items.topic: Therapeutic communication — reflection restates the client’s words to show active listening
items.stem: A client says, “Nobody on this unit listens to me.” Which nurse response best uses reflection (restating) as a therapeutic communication technique?

options.text: “You’re feeling as though staff are not listening to you.”
“You shouldn’t feel that way—everyone here cares about you.”
“Let’s talk about your discharge plans instead.”
“Why are you being so negative about the nurses?”

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: reflection restates what the patient said so they hear their own words, encourages continued communication, and shows active listening. OpenStax PMH emphasizes active listening to capture meaning without judgment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Minimizing/false reassurance is a nontherapeutic barrier.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Changing the subject is a barrier to therapeutic communication.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Asking “why” can feel accusatory and is generally nontherapeutic.

items.topic: NGN matrix — reflection/active listening vs nontherapeutic barriers
items.stem: For a client who states, “I feel invisible here,” indicate whether each nurse response is Indicated (therapeutic reflection/active listening) or Not indicated (nontherapeutic barrier).

rows.text: Restate: “You’re feeling as though you’re not being noticed.”
Offer presence and encourage elaboration (e.g., “Go on…” / sit and listen)
Change the subject to unit meal times to cheer the client up
Say, “Don’t worry—everyone feels that way sometimes; you’ll be fine.”
Ask, “Why do you always complain about the staff?”

rationales.R1: Indicated. Reflection restates the client’s message to show active listening.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Active listening / offering self supports continued communication.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Changing the subject is a barrier.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. False reassurance/minimizing is nontherapeutic.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Accusatory “why” questions are nontherapeutic.

items.jurisdiction_note: OpenStax Maternal-Newborn concordant with Ontario hospital postpartum teaching (NYGH)
items.topic: Postpartum sitz bath — warm shallow soak without soap; pat dry
items.stem: A postpartum client with perineal discomfort after vaginal birth asks how to use a sitz bath at home. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Prepare a warm shallow bath; sit in water without soap for about 10–15 minutes up to three times daily, then gently pat the perineum dry
Add bubble bath and scrub vigorously with a washcloth after each soak
Use only ice water for 45 minutes continuously once a day
Fill the basin with hot undiluted antiseptic and leave the area wet without drying

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: warm shallow bath without soap, soak up to three times/day for 10–15 minutes, gently pat dry; do not add additives unless instructed. NYGH: warm water, do not add soap/bubble bath; sit ~10 minutes ≥3 times/day; pat dry, do not rub.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Soap/bubble bath is not advised; rubbing can irritate healing tissue.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Guidance is warm (not ice-only prolonged) soaks for comfort/healing; ice packs are a separate early measure.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Do not add chemicals unless instructed; pat dry after soaking.

items.topic: Seat belts — buckle up every trip, every seat; air bags are not a substitute
items.stem: A community health nurse teaches adult vehicle-occupant safety. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Wear a seat belt in front and rear seats on every trip, no matter how short; air bags add protection but do not replace seat belts
Seat belts are unnecessary for trips under 5 minutes in residential areas
Rear-seat passengers do not need seat belts if the driver is belted
Air bags alone provide complete crash protection, so seat belts are optional

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: use a seat belt every trip, no matter how short, including back seats; air bags are not a substitute. Transport Canada: buckle up every time, every trip; passengers must always wear seat belts.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Short trips still require buckling up.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rear-seat occupants should buckle up as well.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Air bags complement—not replace—seat belts.

items.topic: Verbal/telephone orders — record and read back for confirmation (closed loop)
items.stem: A provider gives a telephone medication order. Which nursing action best reduces miscommunication risk?

options.text: Record the complete order and read it back to the provider for confirmation (closed-loop read-back)
Memorize the order and administer immediately without documenting until the end of the shift
Repeat only the drug name aloud and assume the dose is the usual one for that drug
Enter a different dose than stated if it seems safer, without clarifying with the provider

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ PSNet: recipients should record and read back verbal orders; read-back verifies hearing and transcription. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS check-back example: nurse records telephone order and reads it back; provider confirms “Correct.”
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delayed documentation increases transcription/memory error risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Full order elements must be verified, not assumed.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Do not silently change orders; clarify/confirm with the provider.

items.topic: NGN cloze — verbal order closed-loop read-back steps
items.stem: Complete the statement about safe telephone/verbal medication-order communication.

ngn.template: The nurse should {B1} the complete order and {B2} to the provider so the provider can {B3}.

B2.text: omit the dose to save time
change the route silently if preferred

B3.text: confirm it is correct (close the loop)
ask the nurse to invent a dose

rationales.B1a: Correct. Record/enter the complete order so transcription can be verified on read-back.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Memorizing without recording increases error risk.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Delayed documentation undermines timely verification.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Clarify incomplete elements; do not silently delete them.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Read-back communicates the recorded order to the sender for verification.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. The full order—not only the class—must be verified.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Dose is a critical order element requiring confirmation.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Do not silently change routes; clarify with the provider.
rationales.B3a: Correct. Provider confirmation closes the TeamSTEPPS check-back loop.
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. Lack of confirmation leaves the loop open.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Doses must come from the ordering provider.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries / Dear CNO self-disclosure guidance for Ontario practice
items.topic: CNO — limited brief self-disclosure only when therapeutic; keep focus on client
items.stem: An Ontario nurse considers sharing personal details to support an anxious client. According to CNO guidance on self-disclosure, which approach is appropriate?

options.text: If used, keep disclosure brief and relevant to the client’s needs, then immediately return the focus to the client’s care
Share extensive details about the nurse’s own illness and family problems so the client can comfort the nurse
Use self-disclosure mainly to meet the nurse’s need for emotional support during the shift
Discuss whatever personal topics the client asks about without limit

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Dear CNO / case scenarios: limited self-disclosure may be appropriate if brief, relevant, and immediately returns focus to the client. Excessive disclosure can shift focus, create dependence, and cross boundaries. OpenStax PMH: limit self-disclosure within professional boundaries.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Detailed personal sharing that shifts the client into comforting the nurse is a boundary concern.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Disclosure must address the client’s therapeutic needs, not the nurse’s personal needs.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nurses must remain mindful of how much they disclose.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO self-disclosure / boundary guidance for Ontario practice
items.topic: NGN cloze — CNO self-disclosure brief, relevant, return focus to client
items.stem: Complete the statement about CNO-aligned therapeutic self-disclosure.

ngn.template: When self-disclosure is used, it should be {B1} and {B2}, and the nurse should then {B3}.

B1.text: focused on the nurse’s unrelated family conflicts
long enough for the client to counsel the nurse

B2.text: intended mainly to vent the nurse’s stress
designed to make the client comfort the nurse
unrelated to the reason for the visit

B3.text: return the focus to the client’s care and re-establish boundaries if needed
continue sharing until the client asks for a personal phone number
ask the client to counsel the nurse about personal problems
accept a social-media friend request to deepen rapport

rationales.B1a: Correct. CNO: keep self-disclosure brief when it is used.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Extensive personal detail can be a boundary crossing.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Focus must remain therapeutic for the client.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. The client should not be placed in a counseling role for the nurse.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Disclosure must be relevant to the client’s therapeutic needs.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Meeting the nurse’s personal needs is inappropriate.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Clients should not be positioned to comfort the nurse.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Irrelevant personal sharing redirects care.
rationales.B3a: Correct. Return focus to the client; re-establish boundaries when necessary.
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. Personal contact sharing crosses boundaries.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Dual role reversal is nontherapeutic.
rationales.B3d: Incorrect. Social-media dual relationships are inappropriate.

items.topic: Dementia wandering safety — ID bracelet/medical ID and prevention supports
items.stem: A family caregiver asks how to reduce harm if a person with advanced dementia wanders. Which teaching is the priority safety recommendation?

options.text: Have the person wear an ID/medical bracelet (or necklace) with name, address/phone, and caregiver contact information
Leave car keys in plain sight by the door so the person can drive home independently
Remove all door/window alarms because they are too noisy
Avoid telling neighbors about wandering risk to protect privacy completely

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: wear ID bracelet/necklace with name, address, phone, and caretaker contact. NIA: medical bracelet with name/address and caregiver phone number; label clothes if bracelet may be removed.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Keep car keys out of sight to reduce unsafe departure.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Door/window alarms are recommended prevention supports.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Informing neighbors is recommended so they can help if wandering occurs.

items.topic: NGN matrix — dementia wandering prevention/safety actions indicated vs not
items.stem: For a home-dwelling older adult with dementia and wandering risk, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Ensure the person wears an ID/medical bracelet with contact information
Place door/window alarms or STOP signs on exit doors
Keep car keys out of sight
Leave the person with advanced dementia alone at home for long periods
Hide all identification so strangers cannot learn the person’s name

rationales.R1: Indicated. ID/medical bracelet supports safe return if lost.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Alarms/STOP signs help prevent unnoticed exits.
rationales.R3: Indicated. Keep keys out of sight.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Do not leave a person with advanced dementia alone.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Identification is needed for safe return—not concealment of ID.

items.topic: TED/compression stockings — smooth wrinkles; nonslip footwear when ambulating
items.stem: An older adult is taught to use ordered thromboembolic deterrent (TED) hose after surgery. Which teaching is correct?

options.text: Apply as instructed, smooth out wrinkles, and avoid walking without assistance or nonslip socks/shoes to prevent falls
Leave large wrinkles at the ankles because wrinkles improve compression
Walk freely in stocking feet on polished floors without nonslip footwear
Roll the top tightly as a tourniquet band to keep the stocking from slipping

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Med-Surg: instruct how to put TED hose on, smooth out wrinkles, and not walk without assistance or nonslip socks to avoid falling. TRU HCA: anti-embolism stockings promote venous return; ensure no wrinkles.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Wrinkles should be smoothed out.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Nonslip footwear/assistance is taught to prevent falls.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Rolling/tight banding can impair circulation; not recommended teaching.
